title: Treasury auction cycle and the month-end bond trade
ask: Do Treasury auctions or month-ends pay in ETFs?
reason: Both below the bars set in advance.
hypothesis: Treasury ETFs cheapen before auctions and recover after, and long bonds earn a premium over month-end.
question: Treasury notes and bonds have been found to cheapen in the days before a scheduled auction and recover afterwards. Separately, Treasury trading surges on the last day of each month. Does either show up strongly enough in the ETFs we already trade (IEF, TLT, hedged with SHY) to pay for itself, with orders at the next open?
prior: The auction result comes from 1980–2008 data, so nearly all of our 2007–2026 window is out of sample. Calendar effects are easy to keep free of look-ahead, but also among the most mined rules in finance, so the bar was set high: mean gross return of at least 28 bp per round trip to go on, and a deflated Sharpe counted against 9,500 calendar rules.
citations: Lou, D., Yan, H. & Zhang, J. (2013). Anticipated and Repeated Shocks in Liquid Markets. Review of Financial Studies 26(8), 1891–1912.
Sullivan, R., Timmermann, A. & White, H. (2001). Dangers of data mining: the case of calendar effects in stock returns. Journal of Econometrics 105(1), 249–286.
Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Liberty Street Economics (2024). End-of-Month Liquidity in the Treasury Market.
method: Auction dates from Treasury's Fiscal Data auction records (2,793 note and bond auctions), checked against Treasury's published cadence by tenor and year, with reopenings separated from new issues. 10-year auctions trade IEF; 20- and 30-year auctions trade TLT.

Auction pair: a duration-neutral pair (short the target ETF, long its trailing 252-day beta in SHY) from five days before the auction to the auction day, then reversed for six days. A pre-auction window never starts before the auction was announced. 2009 on.
Month-end trade: long TLT from the open two trading days before month-end to the open of the next month's first trading day. 2007 on.

Three variants written down in advance (the auction pair on every auction, the same on new issues only, and the month-end trade). Kill test first: mean gross return per round trip below 14 bp stops a variant; 28 bp is needed to go on to the full gate. Costs 7 bps per unit traded.
verdict_reason: All three variants stopped at the kill test, so the full gate never ran. The auction pair on every auction averaged +3.9 bp gross per round trip (998 trips, t +1.0); on new issues only, +13.5 bp (t +1.9), just under the 14 bp line. The cycle is visible for new issues, where both the cheapening before the auction (+15 bp) and the recovery after it (+12 bp) are positive, mostly in TLT, but not for reopenings. Either way the SHY hedge costs far more than the trade earns. The month-end TLT trade was the strongest: +27.3 bp gross (t +2.9, +13.3 bp net), but uneven over time (+43.6 bp in 2007–2014, +6.1 bp in 2015–2020, +26.6 bp since 2021) and under the 28 bp bar set in advance for a heavily mined calendar rule, so it did not go on. Correction, 2026-10-19: the first run read open prices from the wrong dates; these are the corrected numbers, and no verdict changed.
lessons: The auction cycle showed up only where it should be strongest, in new long-bond issues, and was still too small to pay for a hedged ETF trade.

A duration-neutral pair built from ETFs is costly to trade. TLT moves about six and a half times as much as SHY, so hedging it means trading about fifteen units per round trip, about 107 bp in costs against 4–14 bp gross.
We found a bug in our own first run (open prices read from the wrong dates) by rebuilding one number from raw prices in a second script. The fix moved every number and changed none of the verdicts.
